title: On the Physiological and Historical Importance of Nasal Breathing
text: Nasal breathing is superior to mouth breathing, filtering the air, warming it and humidifying it, and producing nitric oxide that dilates blood vessels and increases oxygen absorption by 10-15% [57]. Ancient practices like yoga and pranayama have recognized its centrality for millennia, unlike the modern tendency toward mouth breathing that has contributed to airway narrowing and problems such as obstructive sleep apnea.
book: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
author: James Nestor

title: On the Negative Consequences of Chronic Mouth Breathing
text: Chronic mouth breathing is associated with a range of health issues, including airway narrowing, snoring, sleep apnea, increased risk of cavities and worsening asthma [20]. Studies have shown that sleeping with the mouth open can reduce lung capacity and alter the oral microbiome, compromising overall health.
book: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
author: James Nestor

title: On Slow, Controlled Breathing for Well-being
text: Slow, deep breathing with about 5.5 seconds for the inhale and 5.5 seconds for the exhale (around 5.5 breaths per minute) optimizes gas exchange and stimulates the vagus nerve, activating the parasympathetic nervous system [217]. This reduces stress, improves heart rate variability and optimizes lung efficiency, as shown by studies of long-lived populations.
book: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
author: James Nestor

title: On Nitric Oxide and Its Benefits from Nasal Breathing
text: Nitric oxide, produced abundantly in the paranasal sinuses during nasal breathing, is a powerful vasodilator that improves circulation, lowers blood pressure, and has antibacterial and antiviral properties [57]. Its importance is such that a deficit caused by mouth breathing is linked to hypertension and endothelial dysfunction.
book: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
author: James Nestor

title: On Dopamine and the Reward Circuit
text: Dopamine drives pleasure and motivation. Adderall spikes it 1000% — but rapid surges desensitize D2 receptors, reducing sensitivity to natural rewards. This 'dopamine captivity' is addiction's core mechanism.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Pleasure-Pain Balance (Hedonic Homeostasis)
text: The brain balances pleasure and pain like a seesaw. Every pleasure tilt triggers an equal opposite correction — prolonged stimulation costs you a period of dysphoria afterward.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Addiction in the Modern Era
text: Lembke calls the smartphone a 'modern hypodermic needle' delivering 24/7 digital dopamine. Alcohol addiction diagnoses rose 50% in elderly, 84% in women — our environment breeds compulsive consumption.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Anhedonia and the Hedonism Paradox
text: Pursuing pleasure for its own sake leads to anhedonia — the inability to feel any pleasure. Drug abuse shrinks D2 receptors and dopamine release, making nothing feel rewarding anymore.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On the Dopamine Fast
text: A month-long abstinence from dopamine triggers can reset the neural set point. Works for ~80% of patients, restoring sensitivity to natural rewards and reducing compulsive cravings.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Self-Binding and Moderation
text: Self-binding strategies limit access to high-dopamine behaviors — time-based ('no weed before 9am') or categorical ('gluten-free' to cut calorie-dense carbs). Moderation requires deliberate barriers.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Pain's Role and the Pursuit of Discomfort
text: Embracing pain can yield lasting pleasure: cold water immersion boosts dopamine 250% and norepinephrine 530%. Voluntary discomfort rebalances the hedonic seesaw naturally.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Shrinking Time Horizons in Addiction
text: Addicts lose the ability to value future rewards — active users show drastically shortened temporal horizons, choosing immediate hits over long-term gains. Recovery restores future-oriented thinking.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On the Medicalization of Humanity and Emotional Numbing
text: Widespread use of antidepressants and anxiolytics may be stripping essential parts of our humanity. Over-medicalization of emotional experiences risks turning normal suffering into pathology.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D

title: On Human Connection and Oxytocin as Antidote
text: Oxytocin — the bonding hormone — counters addiction's isolating effects. Research shows it increases brain dopamine, suggesting genuine human connection may be the most sustainable reward pathway.
author: Anna Lembke, M.D
